---
title: "Portfolio choice"
subtitle: "Lecture 13"
---

## Overview

By the end of this lecture you can replace a portfolio manager's point estimate of
expected returns and their covariance with the full posterior predictive distribution,
and say how much of a confident-looking allocation was really just uncompensated risk.

::: {.callout-important}
## The result of this chapter

For an investor with risk aversion $\gamma$ who summarises beliefs about next period's
return by its posterior predictive mean $\mu_{\text{pred}}$ and covariance
$\Sigma_{\text{pred}}$, the expected-utility-maximising weights are

$$
w^\star = \frac{1}{\gamma}\,\Sigma_{\text{pred}}^{-1}\,\mu_{\text{pred}} ,
$$

the same closed form as the textbook mean-variance rule with the predictive moments in
place of the sample moments. The difficulty is that $\Sigma_{\text{pred}}$ is never the
sample covariance itself. It is always at least as large, by an amount that depends on
how much data went into estimating it, so the resulting weights are correspondingly
smaller and less levered than a rule that treats the sample moments as the truth.
:::

After working through this chapter you can

1. derive the closed-form mean-variance optimal weights under known parameters and CARA
   utility;
2. diagnose why a plug-in point estimate of the mean and covariance carries an expected
   certainty-equivalent loss, and quantify how that loss scales with sample size and
   asset count;
3. derive the posterior predictive distribution of returns under a conjugate
   normal-inverse-Wishart prior and show that it inflates the plug-in covariance by a
   factor no smaller than one;
4. implement the resulting Bayesian weights in Python and compare them against the
   plug-in rule on real factor data;
5. compare four allocation rules in an expanding-window out-of-sample backtest using
   turnover, drawdown and certainty equivalent rather than average return alone;
6. interpret an average-return ranking that reverses under certainty equivalent, and say
   why average return is the wrong scorecard for a risk-averse investor.

Week 13 of 15, paired with the [Week 13 exercise
session](../exercise-sessions/13-portfolio-choice.qmd). The chapter assumes the Normal
linear regression posterior of Lecture 2 and conjugate updating with an unknown variance;
no sampler is needed, because everything here is available in closed form.

## Motivation: a point estimate that bets the house {#sec-motivation}

An investor who has followed the course this far has a posterior for a regression's
coefficients, a shrinkage rule for when there are too many of them, and a filter for when
they move over time. None of that machinery has yet been asked what to do with the
answer, and the question is not academic: every one of those posteriors was built because
somebody intends to act on it. An investor with wealth to allocate across $n$ risky
assets chooses portfolio weights $w$ to maximise expected utility of the resulting
return, $\mathbb{E}[U(w'r)]$, where $r$ is next period's vector of returns. This
separates two distinct ingredients, how returns behave and how much the investor dislikes
risk, and asks the investor to be honest about how well the first of these is really
known before acting on the second. Under constant absolute risk aversion,
$U(x) = -e^{-\gamma x}$, and a Normal return $r \sim N(\mu, \Sigma)$, expected utility
collapses to the mean-variance objective and a closed-form optimum,

$$
w^\star = \frac{1}{\gamma}\, \Sigma^{-1} \mu ,
$$

conditional on knowing $\mu$ and $\Sigma$. In practice we never do. The obvious way to
operationalise the formula is the plug-in rule: replace $\mu$ and $\Sigma$ with the
sample mean and sample covariance and act as if they were the truth, the known-parameter
problem solved at an estimated point rather than the investor's actual problem of
weighing outcomes given everything, including the parameters, that is uncertain. The
chunk below does exactly that on the three Fama-French factors, the market, size and
value, which is the dataset the rest of the chapter uses.

```{python}
#| label: fig-plugin-weights
#| fig-cap: "Plug-in optimal weights on the three Fama-French factors, full sample, against an equal-weight benchmark."
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.figsize": (7, 4.2), "axes.grid": True,
                     "grid.alpha": 0.3, "font.size": 11})

DATA = next(p for p in (Path("data"), Path("../data")) if p.exists())
ff_m = pd.read_parquet(DATA / "ff_factors_monthly.parquet")
F_ff = ff_m.loc["1970-01":, ["mkt_rf", "smb", "hml"]].dropna()
R_ff = F_ff.to_numpy()
T_ff, n_ff = R_ff.shape
mu_ff, S_ff = R_ff.mean(axis=0), np.cov(R_ff, rowvar=False)
gamma = 5.0

def mv_weights(m, cov, gamma):
    return (1.0 / gamma) * np.linalg.solve(cov, m)

w_plug_full = mv_weights(mu_ff, S_ff, gamma)
se_ann = np.sqrt(np.diag(S_ff) / T_ff) * 1200

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
x = np.arange(n_ff)
ax.bar(x - 0.18, w_plug_full, width=0.36, color="C1", label="plug-in optimal")
ax.bar(x + 0.18, np.full(n_ff, 1 / n_ff), width=0.36, color="grey", label="equal weight")
ax.axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.8)
ax.set_xticks(x); ax.set_xticklabels(F_ff.columns)
ax.set_ylabel("portfolio weight")
ax.set_title("The plug-in rule bets far more on value than an equal-weight benchmark")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"{T_ff} months, {F_ff.index[0]:%Y-%m} to {F_ff.index[-1]:%Y-%m}")
print("plug-in weights:", np.round(w_plug_full, 3))
print(f"gross leverage (sum |w|): {np.abs(w_plug_full).sum():.2f}")
print("annualised standard error of the sample mean, % p.a.:", np.round(se_ann, 2))
```

The plug-in rule asks for 0.731 in the market, 0.003 in size and 0.903 in value, a gross
leverage of 1.638, meaning $1.64 of factor exposure is taken for every euro of wealth
once the short and long legs are added up. The value position is larger than the market
position, which is the first warning sign: the annualised standard error of value's
sample mean is about 1.4 percentage points, so a large chunk of the confidence expressed
in that 0.903 is standard error rather than signal. Size, whose sample mean is close to
zero and whose standard error is of similar size, gets almost no weight at all, 0.003,
which already hints at the pattern the rest of the chapter will make precise: the rule is
not shy about betting on an estimate, it is only shy when the estimate itself is close to
zero. Nothing here is a matrix-inversion pathology of the kind Lecture 6 diagnosed for a
badly conditioned design; with only three, weakly correlated assets the sample covariance
is perfectly well behaved, so whatever goes wrong below comes from treating an estimated
mean as if it were known, not from inverting a nearly singular matrix.

The question this raises is not rhetorical. A rule that looks this confident either earns
its confidence out of sample or it does not, and the rest of the chapter answers that
question rather than asserting it. The answer, worked out in the empirical section below,
is that the plug-in rule loses money relative to simpler and more modest alternatives once
it has to trade on data it has not yet seen: a large expected-return advantage on paper
does not survive being scored on the criterion the investor actually cares about, which is
not how much a portfolio earned but how much certain, risk-adjusted return it delivered.
That distinction, between an average outcome and its certainty-equivalent value, is what
the rest of the chapter is about, and it is worth stating precisely once before it is used
repeatedly: the certainty equivalent of a weight $w$ is the risk-free return that would
leave the investor equally satisfied, $w'\mu - \tfrac{\gamma}{2}w'\Sigma w$, and it is
smaller than the average return whenever the position carries risk, by an amount that
grows with both risk aversion and the variance actually taken on.

## The problem: what a point estimate costs, in expectation {#sec-problem}

### Result R-13.1: the expected loss from plugging in a point estimate

Fix true parameters $\mu$ and $\Sigma$ and let $w^\star = \Sigma^{-1}\mu/\gamma$ be the
optimal weight. The certainty equivalent of any weight $w$, the risk-free return that
would leave a mean-variance investor equally well off, is
$\mathrm{CE}(w) = w'\mu - \tfrac{\gamma}{2}w'\Sigma w$, and the loss from using $w$
instead of $w^\star$ is exactly quadratic,

$$
L(w) \;=\; \mathrm{CE}(w^\star) - \mathrm{CE}(w) \;=\; \frac{\gamma}{2}\,(w - w^\star)'\Sigma\,(w - w^\star),
$$

with no approximation anywhere: the loss is exactly quadratic in the weight error for any
weight, not only for one close to the optimum. For the plug-in rule
$\hat w = \Sigma^{-1}\hat\mu/\gamma$ built from $T$ independent draws with $\Sigma$ known,
the expected loss is

$$
\mathbb{E}\big[L(\hat w)\big] \;=\; \frac{n}{2\gamma T},
$$

increasing in the number of assets and falling at rate $1/T$: waiting for more data helps,
but only slowly, and a richer asset universe makes the plug-in rule worse before it makes
it better. Estimating $\Sigma$ as well as $\mu$ makes the loss larger still.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

Expand $\mathrm{CE}(w)$ around $w^\star$. Writing $w = w^\star + d$,

$$
\mathrm{CE}(w) = (w^\star+d)'\mu - \frac{\gamma}{2}(w^\star+d)'\Sigma(w^\star+d)
= \mathrm{CE}(w^\star) + d'\mu - \gamma\,d'\Sigma w^\star - \frac{\gamma}{2}d'\Sigma d .
$$

Since $\Sigma w^\star = \Sigma\Sigma^{-1}\mu/\gamma = \mu/\gamma$, the middle term is
$\gamma\, d'\Sigma w^\star = d'\mu$, which exactly cancels the linear term $d'\mu$. What
remains is $L(w) = \tfrac{\gamma}{2}d'\Sigma d$, the displayed quadratic loss.

Apply this with $d = \hat w - w^\star = \Sigma^{-1}(\hat\mu - \mu)/\gamma$, so that

$$
d'\Sigma d = \frac{1}{\gamma^2}(\hat\mu-\mu)'\Sigma^{-1}\Sigma\Sigma^{-1}(\hat\mu-\mu)
= \frac{1}{\gamma^2}(\hat\mu-\mu)'\Sigma^{-1}(\hat\mu-\mu).
$$

With $T$ i.i.d. observations, $\hat\mu \sim N(\mu, \Sigma/T)$, so
$T(\hat\mu-\mu)'\Sigma^{-1}(\hat\mu-\mu)$ is a $\chi^2_n$ variable with mean $n$. Hence

$$
\mathbb{E}[L(\hat w)] = \frac{\gamma}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{\gamma^2}\cdot\frac{n}{T}
= \frac{n}{2\gamma T},
$$

the displayed result. The loss is linear in $n$ because each badly estimated coordinate of
$\mu$ contributes its own independent piece of $\chi^2_n$, and it is proportional to
$1/\gamma$ because a more risk-averse investor scales the whole position down and a
smaller position makes a smaller mistake. When $\Sigma$ is also estimated the same
argument no longer gives an exact closed form, because $\hat\Sigma^{-1}$ is a nonlinear,
biased function of the data, but the loss can only grow: the plug-in rule now inverts an
estimated matrix as well as a mispositioned mean, and inversion is where the small errors
of Lecture 6 get amplified.
:::

The formula is a claim about any true $(\mu,\Sigma)$, so it can be checked by treating the
factors' own sample moments as if they were the truth and simulating from them.

```{python}
#| label: fig-ce-loss-theory
#| fig-cap: "Expected certainty-equivalent loss of the plug-in rule against the theoretical formula n/(2 gamma T), using the Fama-French sample moments as the truth."
w_opt_ff = mv_weights(mu_ff, S_ff, gamma)
ce_star_ff = float(w_opt_ff @ mu_ff - 0.5 * gamma * (w_opt_ff @ S_ff @ w_opt_ff))

def ce_at_truth(w):
    return float(w @ mu_ff - 0.5 * gamma * (w @ S_ff @ w))

sizes_ff = [24, 36, 60, 120, 240, 480]
loss_rows = []
for T_s in sizes_ff:
    lp, le = [], []
    for _ in range(400):
        R_s = rng.multivariate_normal(mu_ff, S_ff, size=T_s)
        lp.append(ce_star_ff - ce_at_truth(
            mv_weights(R_s.mean(axis=0), np.cov(R_s, rowvar=False), gamma)))
        le.append(ce_star_ff - ce_at_truth(np.full(n_ff, 1 / n_ff)))
    loss_rows.append({"T": T_s, "plug-in": np.mean(lp) * 1200,
                      "equal weight": np.mean(le) * 1200,
                      "theory n/(2 gamma T)": n_ff / (2 * gamma * T_s) * 1200})
loss_tab = pd.DataFrame(loss_rows).set_index("T")

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(sizes_ff, loss_tab["plug-in"], "o-", color="C1", label="plug-in")
ax.plot(sizes_ff, loss_tab["equal weight"], "o-", color="C2", label="equal weight")
ax.plot(sizes_ff, loss_tab["theory n/(2 gamma T)"], "k--", lw=1.2,
        label=r"theory $n/(2\gamma T)$, known $\Sigma$")
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("estimation sample length T, months")
ax.set_ylabel("expected certainty-equivalent loss, % per year")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"maximum attainable certainty equivalent: {ce_star_ff*1200:.3f} % p.a.")
print(loss_tab.round(3))
```

At $T = 24$ months the plug-in rule loses 26.174 percentage points a year against a maximum
attainable certainty equivalent of 4.43, which is to say it does not merely fail to reach
the target but destroys several times that much: with two years of data the sample mean
is so poorly pinned down that the rule takes a confident position on noise and pays for
it. The loss falls to 3.56 points at $T = 120$, the length used to start the backtest
below, and to 0.77 by $T = 480$, tracing out the $1/T$ decline the formula predicts. The
dashed theory line sits below the plug-in curve everywhere, and the gap is largest at
small $T$: the formula prices only the mean's estimation error, and the extra distance is
the additional cost, not covered by R-13.1 as stated, of also estimating and inverting the
covariance, which is exactly the estimation error that a badly conditioned design
amplifies, as in Lecture 6, except that here the amplification comes from a small sample
rather than a collinear one. The equal-weight rule, which estimates nothing, has a loss
that does not depend on $T$ at all and crosses the plug-in curve between $T=240$ and
$T=480$: below about twenty years of monthly data, not optimising is the better choice.
That crossing is the puzzle the rest of the chapter tries to repair rather than concede,
because refusing to use the data at all cannot be the intended lesson of a course about
using it correctly.

## Methodology: weights from the predictive distribution, not the point estimate {#sec-methodology}

The repair is to stop conditioning on a single value of $(\mu,\Sigma)$ and instead
integrate the return distribution over everything the posterior finds plausible for them,
exactly the move that turned an intractable point estimate into a defensible answer in
every earlier chapter of this course. The relevant object is the posterior predictive
distribution of next period's return,

$$
p(r_{T+1}\mid\text{data}) = \int p(r_{T+1}\mid\mu,\Sigma)\,p(\mu,\Sigma\mid\text{data})\,d\mu\,d\Sigma,
$$

which averages the return distribution over everything the data leave plausible for
$(\mu,\Sigma)$ rather than freezing them at their most likely values. Nothing about this
step is specific to portfolios: it is the same predictive integral that turned a
regression coefficient's uncertainty into a wider forecast interval in Lecture 2 and a
volatility path's uncertainty into a wider option price in Lecture 12. What is specific to
this chapter is what comes next, because an investor does not read off a predictive
interval and stop; a predictive distribution is only useful here once it has been fed
through a decision rule. The first result says what the integration in the display above
does to the distribution being maximised against; the second says what it then does to
the weights themselves.

### Result R-13.2: the posterior predictive distribution and its inflated covariance

Let $r \mid \mu,\Sigma \sim N(\mu,\Sigma)$ with the conjugate normal-inverse-Wishart prior
$\mu \mid \Sigma \sim N(m_0, \Sigma/k_0)$, $\Sigma \sim IW(\nu_0, S_0)$, the natural
multivariate generalisation of the Normal-inverse-gamma prior this course has used since
Lecture 2, with $k_0$ playing the role of the prior sample size that $B_0^{-1}$ played
there and $\nu_0,S_0$ the role $\alpha_0,\delta_0$ played for a single variance. After $T$
observations the posterior is again normal-inverse-Wishart with parameters $k_T = k_0+T$,
$\nu_T = \nu_0+T$, a mean $m_T$ that pools the prior mean and the sample mean, and a
scatter $S_T$ that pools the prior scatter, the sample scatter and a term penalising a
sample mean that sits far from the prior one. Averaging the return distribution over this
posterior gives a predictive distribution that is multivariate Student-$t$,

$$
r_{T+1} \mid \text{data} \;\sim\; t_{\nu_T-n+1}\Big(m_T, \; \Sigma_{\text{pred}}\Big),
\qquad
\Sigma_{\text{pred}} = \Big(1+\frac{1}{k_T}\Big)\frac{S_T}{\nu_T-n-1} ,
$$

strictly larger, in the positive semi-definite order, than the plug-in covariance
$S_T/(\nu_T-n-1)$ for any finite $k_T$, and converging to it only as $k_T \to \infty$.
The number $k_T$ plays the same role here that a sample size plays everywhere else in
this course: it measures how much has been learned, whether from data or from a prior
that behaves as if it were $k_0$ observations, and the predictive distribution never
forgets that some of what it knows is still an estimate. Two features of the result are
worth stating plainly before the algebra. First, the inflation applies to every direction
of the covariance at once and by the same scalar factor, so it changes the overall scale
of the uncertainty an investor should attribute to returns without changing the relative
riskiness of one asset against another. Second, the inflation is largest exactly when the
sample is smallest, which is the mirror image of R-13.1: the same shortage of data that
makes the plug-in point estimate unreliable also tells the predictive distribution to
widen itself, and the two effects are two views of one fact rather than two separate
corrections that happen to point the same way.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

Work first with a single asset, so that the prior is $\beta\mid\sigma^2\sim N(b_0,\sigma^2/k_0)$,
$\sigma^2\sim IG(\alpha_0,\delta_0)$, and the model is $r_t=\beta+\varepsilon_t$,
$\varepsilon_t\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$. Completing the square in $\beta$ against $T$
observations gives $\beta\mid\sigma^2,r\sim N(b_T,\sigma^2/k_T)$ with $k_T=k_0+T$ and
$b_T=(k_0b_0+T\bar r)/k_T$, and collecting the remaining terms gives
$\sigma^2\mid r\sim IG(\alpha_T,\delta_T)$ with $\alpha_T=\alpha_0+T/2$. Conditional on
$\sigma^2$, a new draw is $r_{T+1}=\beta+\varepsilon_{T+1}$ with $\varepsilon_{T+1}$ a
fresh, independent shock, so $r_{T+1}\mid\sigma^2,r\sim N(b_T,\sigma^2(1+1/k_T))$: one
unit of unavoidable shock variance plus $1/k_T$ of a unit from not knowing $\beta$.
Integrating $\sigma^2$ out against its inverse-gamma posterior turns the Normal kernel
into a Student-$t$ kernel with $2\alpha_T$ degrees of freedom, by the standard
Normal-inverse-gamma mixture argument, and the scale absorbs the factor $1+1/k_T$
unchanged. Sending the prior on $\beta$ to flat, $k_0\to0$, gives $k_T\to T$ and recovers
the familiar $1+1/T$ inflation of the sample mean's forecast variance.

The matrix version replaces the same three steps with matrices. Multiplying the Normal
likelihood by the Normal-inverse-Wishart prior and completing the square in $\mu$ gives a
Normal posterior for $\mu$ given $\Sigma$ with precision $k_T\Sigma^{-1}$ centred at $m_T$,
and the leftover terms give an inverse-Wishart posterior for $\Sigma$ with degrees of
freedom $\nu_T$ and scale matrix $S_T$, the prior scatter plus the sample scatter plus a
term $\tfrac{k_0T}{k_T}(\bar r-m_0)(\bar r-m_0)'$ that penalises a sample mean far from the
prior mean. Conditional on $\Sigma$, a new draw has covariance $\Sigma(1+1/k_T)$ by the
same shock-plus-parameter-uncertainty argument as the scalar case. Averaging over the
inverse-Wishart posterior for $\Sigma$, whose mean is $S_T/(\nu_T-n-1)$, replaces $\Sigma$
by its posterior mean and turns the Normal into a multivariate Student-$t$ with
$\nu_T-n+1$ degrees of freedom, giving the displayed $\Sigma_{\text{pred}}$. Because
$1+1/k_T>1$ for every finite $k_T$, the predictive covariance strictly exceeds the
plug-in one along every direction, and the gap closes only as $k_T$ grows, exactly the
pattern that $B_T\to0$ traces out for the coefficient posterior itself.
:::

### Result R-13.3: optimal weights under parameter uncertainty, and pure de-levering

Maximising $w'\mu_{\text{pred}} - \tfrac{\gamma}{2}w'\Sigma_{\text{pred}}w$ over $w$ gives
the closed form stated in the Overview, $w^\star = \Sigma_{\text{pred}}^{-1}\mu_{\text{pred}}/\gamma$.
Whenever the predictive covariance is a scalar multiple of the plug-in one,
$\Sigma_{\text{pred}} = \kappa S$ with $\kappa>1$, the two rules choose the same direction:

$$
w^\star_{\text{pred}} = \frac{1}{\gamma}(\kappa S)^{-1}\mu = \frac{1}{\kappa}\,w^\star_{\text{plug}} ,
$$

so parameter uncertainty is pure de-levering, scaling every weight down by the same
factor without changing which asset is long and which is short. Once the prior mean
$m_0$ differs from the sample mean, $\mu_{\text{pred}}$ is itself shrunk toward $m_0$ and
the direction of the portfolio changes as well, not only its size. This distinction
matters for interpreting anything measured later: a change in leverage with the same
proportions across assets is R-13.2 alone at work, while a change that also rotates the
portfolio toward or away from a particular asset is evidence that the prior mean is doing
something beyond simple insurance.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

Differentiate $f(w)=w'm-\tfrac{\gamma}{2}w'Vw$ with respect to $w$: the first term has
gradient $m$, the second, a quadratic form in symmetric $V$, has gradient $\gamma Vw$.
Setting the gradient to zero gives $w^\star=V^{-1}m/\gamma$, and the second derivative
$-\gamma V$ is negative definite whenever $V\succ0$ and $\gamma>0$, so this is the unique
maximum. Applying the formula with $m=\mu_{\text{pred}}$ and $V=\Sigma_{\text{pred}}$
gives the stated $w^\star$.

Now compare two investors who agree on the mean but disagree on the covariance, one using
$S$ and the other $\Sigma_{\text{pred}}=\kappa S$. Substituting,

$$
w^\star_{\text{pred}} = \frac{1}{\gamma}(\kappa S)^{-1}m = \frac{1}{\kappa}\cdot\frac{1}{\gamma}S^{-1}m
= \frac{1}{\kappa}\,w^\star_{\text{plug}} ,
$$

so every coordinate of $w^\star_{\text{plug}}$ is multiplied by the same scalar $1/\kappa$.
In the diffuse-prior limit of R-13.2, $\kappa=(1+1/k_T)(\nu_T-1)/(\nu_T-n-1)$, which is
greater than one for any finite sample and tends to one as the sample grows, so the amount
of de-levering shrinks exactly as the posterior concentrates. Once the prior mean is not
diffuse, $m_T$ is a weighted average of $m_0$ and the sample mean rather than the sample
mean itself, so $w^\star_{\text{pred}}$ is no longer a rescaling of $w^\star_{\text{plug}}$
along the same ray: the correction now moves the portfolio's direction as well as its
size, and the strength of that move is governed by $k_0$ relative to $T$ exactly as the
tightness of a Minnesota prior is governed by $\lambda_1$ relative to the sample.
:::

Both results are silent about which prior to use. Result R-13.2 fixes the shape of the
correction, an inflation factor bigger than one that shrinks toward one as evidence
accumulates, and Result R-13.3 fixes what that correction does to a decision, a smaller
and possibly redirected position. Neither result says how large $k_0$, $\nu_0$ and $S_0$
should be for a given investor, and neither says whether the correction is large enough
to matter in practice once real trading costs, real horizons and a real dataset are
involved. That is not a gap in the mathematics; it is the same division of labour as
every other conjugate model in this course, where the likelihood and the update rule are
settled once and for all and the prior parameters remain the place where an investor's own
economic judgement enters, exactly as $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ did for the Minnesota
prior in Lecture 6. That choice, and whether the repair is worth its complexity once made,
is what the empirical section below measures rather than asserts.

## Data: the three Fama-French factors since 1970 {#sec-data}

The chapter's dataset is the monthly Fama-French factor file,
`data/ff_factors_monthly.parquet`, restricted to the market, size and value factors from
January 1970 onward, already loaded in @sec-motivation. All three are excess returns on
zero-cost, self-financing positions, so an unconstrained weight of 0.7 on the market is
read directly as leverage, seventy cents of market exposure per euro of wealth, with no
separate accounting for a long or short leg. This is what makes the three factors the
right test bed for a chapter about how much confidence a point estimate deserves, rather
than about how badly a nearly collinear design behaves: whatever damage the plug-in rule
does here has to come from estimating three expected returns, since the covariance matrix
itself is easy to invert, as the next chunk confirms. These three series, and no others,
are used everywhere below.

```{python}
#| label: fig-ff-cumulative
#| fig-cap: "Cumulative growth of one euro invested in each Fama-French factor since 1970, log scale."
desc_ff = pd.DataFrame({
    "mean % p.a.": mu_ff * 1200,
    "vol % p.a.": np.sqrt(np.diag(S_ff)) * np.sqrt(12) * 100,
    "Sharpe p.a.": mu_ff / np.sqrt(np.diag(S_ff)) * np.sqrt(12),
}, index=F_ff.columns)
ev_ff = np.linalg.eigvalsh(S_ff)
print(f"{T_ff} months, {F_ff.index[0]:%Y-%m} to {F_ff.index[-1]:%Y-%m}, {n_ff} assets")
print(desc_ff.round(3))
print(f"condition number of the sample covariance: {ev_ff.max()/ev_ff.min():.2f}")
print(F_ff.corr().round(3))

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for j, nm in enumerate(F_ff.columns):
    ax.plot(F_ff.index, np.cumprod(1 + R_ff[:, j]), lw=1.0, label=nm)
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("date"); ax.set_ylabel("cumulative growth (log scale)")
ax.set_title("The three factors since 1970")
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The market earned 7.50 per cent a year in excess of cash at a volatility of 15.85 per
cent, a Sharpe ratio of 0.473. Value earned 3.74 per cent at a volatility of 10.63, a
Sharpe ratio of 0.351, and size earned almost nothing, 0.96 per cent a year at a
volatility of 10.51, a Sharpe ratio of 0.091 that fifty-seven years of data cannot
distinguish from zero. The condition number of the sample covariance is 2.92, about as
benign as a covariance matrix ever gets, and the correlations are small, 0.275 between
market and size and -0.221 between market and value. This is the easy case for matrix
inversion; whatever the plug-in rule does wrong below is a story about an estimated mean,
not a near-singular covariance. The figure shows why value in particular is the factor
worth watching: its cumulative growth line is not a smooth compounding curve but a series
of long climbs interrupted by sharp collapses, the most visible around 1999 and 2000,
exactly the pattern a mean estimated from more placid decades would fail to anticipate.

## Empirical analysis: an expanding-window backtest of four allocation rules {#sec-empirical}

We first fit the predictive rule of R-13.2 and R-13.3 on the full sample, then test both
rules honestly by giving each one, at every point in time, only the data an investor
would actually have had. The prior parameters $(m_0, k_0, \nu_0, S_0)$ have to be chosen
before any of this can run, and every one of them is a statement an investor is asked to
sign, not a number tuned to make the answer come out well. $m_0=0$ says that before
seeing data no factor is assumed to earn a premium, which is the conservative choice for
an equity-market anomaly literature that has been wrong before. $\nu_0$ and $S_0$ are set
so the prior is centred on a monthly volatility of five per cent, about seventeen per cent
a year, in the right neighbourhood for a diversified equity position without pretending to
know the answer to a decimal place. None of these is tuned to the outcome, and the
backtest that follows never lets any of them see a return from the future.

```{python}
k0_ff, m0_ff = 24.0, np.zeros(n_ff)
nu0_ff, S0_ff = n_ff + 5.0, (n_ff + 5.0) * np.diag(np.full(n_ff, 0.05 ** 2))

def niw_predictive(R_sample):
    T_s, n_s = R_sample.shape
    rbar = R_sample.mean(axis=0)
    scatter = (R_sample - rbar).T @ (R_sample - rbar)
    kT = k0_ff + T_s
    mT = (k0_ff * m0_ff + T_s * rbar) / kT
    nuT = nu0_ff + T_s
    d = (rbar - m0_ff)[:, None]
    ST = S0_ff + scatter + (k0_ff * T_s / kT) * (d @ d.T)
    return mT, ST * (1 + 1 / kT) / (nuT - n_s - 1)

w_bayes_full = mv_weights(*niw_predictive(R_ff), gamma)
print("plug-in:", np.round(w_plug_full, 3), " Bayes predictive:", np.round(w_bayes_full, 3))
print(f"gross leverage: plug-in {np.abs(w_plug_full).sum():.3f}, "
      f"Bayes {np.abs(w_bayes_full).sum():.3f}")
```

The prior is deliberately mild but genuinely informative: a prior mean of zero, so that
before seeing data no factor is assumed to earn a premium, and $k_0=24$, so the prior
carries the weight of two years of data against the sample's fifty-seven. On the full
679-month sample the two rules already differ, plug-in leverage of 1.636 against 1.544
for the Bayes predictive rule, even though with this much data the inflation factor in
R-13.2 is close to one: $k_T = 24+679=703$, so the prior contributes well under four per
cent of the effective sample size, and yet the weight on value still moves from 0.903 to
0.845, because that factor's mean is exactly the case, discussed in R-13.3, where the
prior mean is not diffuse and the correction rotates the portfolio rather than only
shrinking it. That is not a full-sample story on its own. Ten years of data, the length an
investor in 1980 actually had, is where the same mechanism has its largest effect, which is
why the honest test has to be run in an expanding window that starts where the data start
rather than on the full sample alone.

```{python}
burn_ff = 120
w_ew_ff = np.full(n_ff, 1.0 / n_ff)
rule_names = ["plug-in", "Bayes predictive", "shrink to equal weight", "equal weight"]
W_hist = {k: [] for k in rule_names}
r_hist = {k: [] for k in rule_names}
dates_oos = []

for t in range(burn_ff, T_ff):
    R_sub = R_ff[:t]
    w_p = mv_weights(R_sub.mean(axis=0), np.cov(R_sub, rowvar=False), gamma)
    w_b = mv_weights(*niw_predictive(R_sub), gamma)
    w_s = 0.5 * w_p + 0.5 * w_ew_ff
    for name, w in zip(rule_names, [w_p, w_b, w_s, w_ew_ff]):
        W_hist[name].append(w)
        r_hist[name].append(float(w @ R_ff[t]))
    dates_oos.append(F_ff.index[t])
dates_oos = pd.DatetimeIndex(dates_oos)

def max_drawdown(r):
    wealth = np.cumprod(1.0 + np.asarray(r))
    return float((wealth / np.maximum.accumulate(wealth) - 1.0).min())

bt_rows = []
for name in rule_names:
    r = np.array(r_hist[name]); Wk = np.array(W_hist[name])
    bt_rows.append({"strategy": name,
                    "mean % p.a.": r.mean() * 1200,
                    "vol % p.a.": r.std(ddof=1) * np.sqrt(12) * 100,
                    "Sharpe": r.mean() / r.std(ddof=1) * np.sqrt(12),
                    "turnover": np.abs(np.diff(Wk, axis=0)).sum(axis=1).mean(),
                    "max DD %": max_drawdown(r) * 100,
                    "CE % p.a.": (r.mean() - 0.5 * gamma * r.var(ddof=1)) * 1200,
                    "avg leverage": np.abs(Wk).sum(axis=1).mean()})
backtest = pd.DataFrame(bt_rows).set_index("strategy")
print(f"out-of-sample months: {len(dates_oos)}, "
      f"{dates_oos[0]:%Y-%m} to {dates_oos[-1]:%Y-%m}")
print(backtest.round(3).T)
```

The estimation sample always starts in January 1980, so the first ten years of the panel
serve as the burn-in that gives the shortest rule a fighting chance, and the window then
grows one month at a time and never sees the return it is about to be scored on. Four
rules compete: the plug-in, the Bayes predictive, a fifty-fifty blend of the plug-in
weights with equal weights, and equal weights itself, which estimates nothing and is the
benchmark this literature finds hard to beat. Turnover, the average month-to-month change
in gross weight, and the maximum drawdown, the worst peak-to-trough fall in compounded
wealth, are recorded alongside the more familiar mean, volatility and Sharpe ratio because
a rule that looks identical on Sharpe ratio can still be far more expensive to run and far
more painful to hold. Read the table one column at a time, because only one of them is the
investor's actual objective.

The plug-in rule earns the highest average return, 10.21 per cent a year, which is the
number people quote. It also carries the highest volatility, 17.90 per cent, the highest
average leverage, 2.59, the most turnover, and the deepest drawdown, a fall of 68.7 per
cent from peak to trough, meaning an investor who followed it would at some point have
watched more than two thirds of the strategy's peak wealth disappear before it recovered.
Its Sharpe ratio, 0.570, is no better than equal weight's 0.587: all the extra return
came from taking more risk, not from superior information. The Bayes predictive rule
earns 8.73 per cent at 15.63 volatility, cutting average leverage from 2.59 to 2.23 and
the drawdown from 68.7 to 64.4 per cent, with a Sharpe ratio, 0.559, that is again
indistinguishable from the others. The shrunk blend goes further on every one of these
columns at once, 7.13 per cent average return at 11.67 volatility, a Sharpe ratio of
0.611 that is the highest of the four, turnover of only 0.024 and a drawdown of 51.8 per
cent, cut nearly in half relative to the plug-in rule.

The column that decides the question is the certainty equivalent, the mean-variance
investor's own scorecard. The plug-in rule delivers 2.20 per cent a year, the Bayes
predictive rule 2.63, equal weight 2.86, and the blend of plug-in and equal weight 3.72.
Ranking by certainty equivalent reverses the ranking by average return completely.
Integrating over parameter uncertainty bought 0.43 percentage points over the plug-in
rule, about a fifth more; shrinking half way to equal weights bought 1.52 points,
considerably more, because a fifty per cent shrink toward a fixed portfolio is a far
stronger prior than $k_0=24$ months of data. The lesson is not that the Bayesian repair
fails but that the strength of the prior, not its provenance, is what moves the answer.

Turnover tells the same story from a different angle. The plug-in rule trades 0.048 of
gross weight a month on average, the Bayes predictive rule 0.040, a reduction of about
seventeen per cent that follows directly from R-13.3: a rule that is less levered also has
less distance to travel when the estimate updates. Turnover matters because every one of
these numbers is gross of transaction costs, which this chapter does not model; a real
implementation would shave a further, cost-proportional amount off every column, and the
rule that already trades less starts from a smaller handicap.

```{python}
#| label: fig-wealth-paths
#| fig-cap: "Cumulative wealth of four allocation rules on the Fama-French factors, 1980 to 2026, log scale."
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for name, colour in zip(rule_names, ["C1", "C0", "C2", "black"]):
    wealth = np.cumprod(1.0 + np.array(r_hist[name]))
    ax.plot(dates_oos, wealth, color=colour, lw=1.3, label=name)
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("date"); ax.set_ylabel("cumulative excess-return wealth (log scale)")
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

final_wealth = {k: float(np.cumprod(1.0 + np.array(r_hist[k]))[-1]) for k in rule_names}
print({k: round(v, 2) for k, v in final_wealth.items()})
```

The log scale matters. On a linear axis the plug-in path looks like a triumph, a euro
invested in 1980 growing to about 53.6 against 5.9 for equal weight. On a log scale, where
equal vertical distances are equal percentage moves, the plug-in path is visibly the most
violent of the four, with its deepest hole in the 1999 to 2000 stretch when the value
factor collapsed and the rule was heavily long value. The equal-weight path is the
smoothest of the four, never straying far below its own historical peak, and the Bayes
predictive and blended paths sit between the two extremes, closer to equal weight in
their smoothness and closer to plug-in in their eventual level. A path that ends higher
after a 69 per cent drawdown is not obviously the one a risk-averse investor would have
chosen, which is the certainty-equivalent column made visible: a picture that only showed
final wealth would have quietly reintroduced the average-return ranking that the whole
chapter is arguing against.

```{python}
#| label: fig-ce-bars
#| fig-cap: "Annualised certainty equivalent achieved by each of the four rules over the same out-of-sample months."
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(backtest.index, backtest["CE % p.a."],
       color=["C1", "C0", "C2", "black"])
ax.set_ylabel("certainty equivalent, % p.a.")
plt.xticks(rotation=15)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The bars restate the table as a picture and make the reversal impossible to miss: the two
rules with the highest average return, plug-in and the unshrunk Bayes rule, are the two
with the lowest certainty equivalent, and the crude fifty-fifty blend that nobody would
call sophisticated wins outright. Shrinkage of any kind buys insurance against the bad
draws at a small premium paid in the good ones, and here more shrinkage bought more
insurance than the principled amount happened to.

A table over forty-six years hides whether the ranking is stable or is carried by one
turbulent decade. Splitting the out-of-sample months at the year 2000 answers that.

```{python}
mid_ff = dates_oos.searchsorted(pd.Timestamp("2000-01-01"))
decade_rows = []
for label, sl in [("1980-1999", slice(0, mid_ff)), ("2000-2026", slice(mid_ff, None))]:
    row = {"period": label}
    for name in rule_names:
        r = np.array(r_hist[name])[sl]
        row[name] = (r.mean() - 0.5 * gamma * r.var(ddof=1)) * 1200
    decade_rows.append(row)
decade_ce = pd.DataFrame(decade_rows).set_index("period")
print("certainty equivalent by sub-period, % p.a.")
print(decade_ce.round(3))
```

The ranking is not stable across the two halves, and the instability itself is the more
useful finding. Before 2000, with the long value rally of the 1980s and 1990s still
intact, the plug-in rule leads, a certainty equivalent of 6.243 per cent a year against
6.000 for the Bayes predictive rule, 6.060 for the shrunk blend and only 3.538 for equal
weight: when the estimated premium is real and persists, betting on it heavily pays off,
and none of the three ways of tempering that bet matches the plug-in rule's own record.
After 2000, once the value factor's collapse enters every rule's estimation sample and its
later, choppier history has to be forecast from it, the ranking reverses outright. The
plug-in rule's certainty equivalent turns negative, -0.852 per cent a year, the Bayes
predictive rule is barely positive at 0.076, while the shrunk blend holds up at 1.959 and
equal weight best of all at 2.344. The full-sample numbers in the table above are
therefore driven overwhelmingly by this second half: shrinkage of any kind is insurance
that costs a little in a decade when the bet pays off and returns a great deal in a decade
when it does not, and an investor who only watched the 1980s and 1990s would have drawn
exactly the wrong lesson about how much to trust an estimated mean.

The mechanism behind the whole table is visible directly, month by month, in how much each
rule is willing to bet.

```{python}
#| label: fig-leverage-time
#| fig-cap: "Gross leverage of the plug-in and Bayes predictive rules over the out-of-sample months, with equal weight's leverage of one marked for reference."
lev_p_ff = np.abs(np.array(W_hist["plug-in"])).sum(axis=1)
lev_b_ff = np.abs(np.array(W_hist["Bayes predictive"])).sum(axis=1)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(dates_oos, lev_p_ff, color="C1", lw=1.1, label="plug-in")
ax.plot(dates_oos, lev_b_ff, color="C0", lw=1.1, label="Bayes predictive")
ax.axhline(1.0, color="black", ls=":", lw=1, label="equal weight")
ax.set_xlabel("date"); ax.set_ylabel("gross leverage, sum of |weights|")
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"gross leverage, plug-in: mean {lev_p_ff.mean():.2f}, max {lev_p_ff.max():.2f}; "
      f"Bayes: mean {lev_b_ff.mean():.2f}, max {lev_b_ff.max():.2f}")
```

The plug-in line sits above the Bayesian one almost everywhere, and both are at their
most extreme in the early 1980s, when the estimation sample was shortest and the value
premium of the previous decade looked enormous relative to how little history had yet
accumulated to temper it. The plug-in rule's peak leverage is above three, three euros of
factor exposure per euro of wealth, which no risk manager would sign off and which the
rule reaches purely because ten years of data made the value premium look larger than it
would turn out to be. The Bayes predictive line is lower everywhere and the two converge
only slowly, exactly the slow $1/T$ closing that R-13.1 and R-13.3 both predict and that
the next section checks directly.

## Discussion: a modest gain, an honest ranking, and a model still linear {#sec-discussion}

The plug-in rule's apparent edge in @sec-motivation was mostly compensation for risk
rather than for information. Once weights are scored by certainty equivalent instead of
average return, integrating over parameter uncertainty turns a losing rule into a
slightly less losing one, a real but modest repair, while the harsher, less principled
shrink toward equal weights does noticeably better on this sample overall. R-13.1 said
the plug-in loss shrinks like $1/T$ and R-13.3 said the correction is largest when the
sample is short; both predictions held up against real trading months, not only against
simulation, in the sense that the Bayes predictive rule's leverage and turnover were
consistently below the plug-in rule's throughout, and by more early in the sample than
late in it, exactly as the theory requires. What the decade split adds is a sharper
caveat: the full-sample certainty-equivalent ranking is not a story that repeats evenly
year after year, it is dominated by one regime change, the value factor's collapse after
1999, in which every de-levered rule was rewarded and the plug-in rule was punished
severely. The honest reading of the certainty-equivalent gap between the Bayes predictive
rule and the cruder blend is not that the derivation in @sec-methodology is wrong;
R-13.2 and R-13.3 are exact statements about what a diffuse-ish conjugate prior does to
the covariance and the weights, and the backtest confirms exactly that mechanism at work
in the leverage figure above. It is that the conjugate prior used here, deliberately mild
so as not to prejudge the answer, is simply a weaker prior than a fifty per cent shrink
toward a fixed portfolio, and a weaker prior corrects a smaller share of the mistake in
the regime where a mistake was there to correct.

The check against something already known is the rate at which the correction fades. R-13.3
says the de-levering factor $1/\kappa$ tends to one as the effective sample size grows, the
same Bernstein-von Mises pattern behind every shrinkage result in this course. That claim
does not need a fresh simulation, because $\kappa=(1+1/k_T)(\nu_T-1)/(\nu_T-n-1)$ is a
closed-form function of $T$ alone.

```{python}
#| label: fig-kappa-decay
#| fig-cap: "The de-levering fraction 1 - 1/kappa implied by R-13.3, as a function of the estimation window length, with the backtest's start and end marked."
T_grid = np.arange(24, 700, 4)
kT = k0_ff + T_grid
nuT = nu0_ff + T_grid
kappa = (1 + 1 / kT) * (nuT - 1) / (nuT - n_ff - 1)
delever = 1 - 1 / kappa

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(T_grid, delever, color="C0")
ax.axvline(burn_ff, color="grey", ls=":", label="backtest start, T=120")
ax.axvline(T_ff, color="black", ls=":", label=f"full sample, T={T_ff}")
ax.set_xlabel("estimation sample length T, months")
ax.set_ylabel("de-levering fraction 1 - 1/kappa")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"de-levering fraction at T=120: {delever[np.searchsorted(T_grid, burn_ff)]:.3f}, "
      f"at T={T_ff}: {delever[-1]:.3f}")
```

At the backtest's first origin the pure covariance-inflation channel of R-13.2 already
de-levers by only about three per cent, and by the end of the sample the fraction is
under one per cent, both far smaller than the five to six per cent gap in average
leverage the full-sample fit above actually showed. The difference between the two
numbers is itself informative, not a contradiction: R-13.3 said the correction is a pure
rescaling only when the prior mean is diffuse, and here it is not, so most of what moves
the weights at long samples is the redirection from an informative prior on the mean
rather than the covariance inflation this figure isolates. The covariance channel alone
shrinks exactly at the rate the derivation predicts, which is the reassurance this course
keeps returning to: a result that only worked in one simulation would be a coincidence,
but a result that predicts, in closed form and ahead of time, how a completely separate
calculation on real trading months will behave is doing what a derivation is supposed to
do.

There is also a limitation no amount of data repairs. Everything in R-13.2 and R-13.3
assumes the object of interest, the vector of expected returns, is summarised by a mean
and covariance that are constant except for what the posterior learns about them; the
investor's belief about the mean return of an asset never depends on anything except how
many months of data went into estimating it. Nothing in the model lets the shape of the
relationship between predictors and returns be anything other than linear. Every model
built in this course so far was linear in the predictors, whether that meant a regression
coefficient in Lecture 2, a lag matrix in Lecture 6, a state that evolves as a linear
autoregression in Lecture 8, or the constant conditional mean assumed here. Lecture 14
asks what happens once that assumption is dropped, and whether letting the mean return
depend nonlinearly on observable signals is worth the loss of a closed form.

## Exercises

These are the chapter's practice questions; the [Week 13 exercise
session](../exercise-sessions/13-portfolio-choice.qmd) works through them and adds the lab.

1. By hand. Starting from R-13.1, show that if $\Sigma$ is also estimated from the same
   $T$ observations by the sample covariance, the expected loss can be written as the
   known-$\Sigma$ term plus a second, non-negative term that depends on the distribution
   of $\hat\Sigma^{-1}-\Sigma^{-1}$. Then, using R-13.3, derive the exact value of
   $\kappa$ at which the plug-in and Bayes predictive rules would choose identical
   weights, and say what that value implies about $k_0$ relative to $T$.

2. Computational. This week's second, moved application asks how a prior belief in the
   CAPM tilts the size and value weights as the prior on each factor's alpha tightens from
   essentially free to essentially dogmatic; the lab in the exercise session sets this up
   using the same three factors and the code of @sec-empirical.

3. On real data. Extend @sec-empirical to five industry portfolios instead of three
   factors, rerun the backtest, and report whether the certainty-equivalent ranking of the
   four rules survives the move to a less well-conditioned covariance matrix, and whether
   the plug-in rule's peak leverage in the early years of the window becomes even more
   extreme once the assets are more numerous and more correlated.

Exercise 1 is the one to attempt before the session, since the exact de-levering
condition is used without comment in the CAPM-tilt lab. Exercises 2 and 3 are written for
the session itself and reuse the functions of @sec-empirical unchanged; both also connect
back to the reference-portfolio shrinkage identity in the reading below, which recasts
the equal-weight blend of @sec-empirical as a regression rather than as an ad hoc average.

## Reading and references

The mean-variance and CARA equivalence recapitulated in @sec-motivation, and the
certainty-equivalent loss behind R-13.1, follow Geweke (2005), Section 2.4, on posterior
expected loss under a stated decision problem rather than a generic accuracy measure. The
closed-form predictive distribution and the de-levering result behind R-13.2 and R-13.3,
and the survey of the wider Bayesian portfolio literature this chapter draws one thread
from, are in Avramov and Zhou (2010). Frey and Pohlmeier (2026), Section 2.2 of the
supplied working paper, is the source of the reference-portfolio shrinkage identity used
in the exercise session, and the CAPM-tilt lab moved there adapts the same regression
machinery introduced in Lecture 2 to the question of how much an investor should let a
pricing theory discipline the data. The explanations and exercises are adapted to this
course's notation and weekly structure; consult the cited originals for the full
treatments and, in the case of the two applications moved to the exercise session, for
worked numbers beyond what the session covers.

Avramov and Zhou (2010), "Bayesian Portfolio Analysis," *Annual Review of Financial
Economics*. Geweke (2005), *Contemporary Bayesian Econometrics and Statistics*. Koop,
*Bayesian Econometrics*, ch. 8. Chan, Koop, Poirier, and Tobias, *Bayesian Econometric
Methods* (2nd ed.), ch. 11.
